name: Rønne
title: Rønne Thickness Measurement | Bornholm Ferries & Wind Vessels
description: Thickness gauging in Rønne, Bornholm, for ro-pax ferries, aluminium fast craft, offshore wind vessels and coasters: hull, deck, tank and piping UTM.
h1: Hull Thickness Gauging for Bornholm Ferries, Fast Craft and Offshore Wind Vessels in Rønne
intro: Rønne is Bornholm's main commercial port and the island's link with the rest of Denmark, Sweden and Germany, served by ro-pax ferries and high-speed catamarans. In recent years the harbour has also been enlarged for the offshore wind industry, which brings installation and project vessels to its quays. Each of these fleets returns to Rønne on a known pattern, so gauging can be planned rather than improvised. For every job, Atlantis sends technicians from India to Bornholm to work on the vessel itself.

highlights.p: The fast craft on the Ystad crossing are aluminium catamarans. Ultrasonic gauging works on aluminium as well as steel, provided the gauge is set up for the alloy's sound velocity, and hull plating, wet-deck structure and waterjet-room spaces make up the usual scope.

The conventional ro-pax ship on the Køge route carries freight and cars on a longer crossing. Its car decks, stern ramp, ballast tanks and machinery-space piping are gauged during planned maintenance stops, timed with the operator around the island's supply needs.

Rønne has served as an installation port for Baltic offshore wind, and installation and heavy-lift vessels use its newer quays. Crane pedestals, sea-fastening areas and deck structure under heavy cargo loads are where crack detection and gauging pay off between campaigns.

port.h: Rønne and the sea routes to Bornholm
p: Bornholm lies in the southern Baltic, far to the east of the rest of Denmark and closer to the coasts of Sweden, Germany and Poland than to Copenhagen. Rønne, on the island's west coast, is its main town and principal port, and almost everything the island consumes or sends away passes over its quays or rolls through its ferry terminal. The harbour faces open water to the west, with breakwaters protecting the basins, and like the rest of the Baltic it has no tidal range worth planning around. Much of the traffic between the western and central Baltic passes through the strait between Bornholm and Sweden, so Rønne sits close to a stream of tankers, bulk carriers and container feeders that seldom stop at the island itself.

The ferry services are the core of the port. High-speed catamarans connect Rønne with Ystad in southern Sweden, from where road and rail continue to Copenhagen, and a conventional ro-pax ferry sails to Køge on Zealand, carrying lorries and cars on a longer passage. In summer a seasonal route to Sassnitz in Germany adds capacity for holiday traffic. Around the ferries, the port handles general cargo, fuel and other bulk supplies for the island, and it receives cruise calls during the summer season. The most visible change in recent years is the expansion of the harbour with new quays, a ro-ro ramp and large project areas, built so that Rønne can serve the offshore wind farms being developed in the southern Baltic.

That expansion has changed the mix of ships. Rønne was chosen as the installation port for the Kriegers Flak offshore wind farm, Denmark's largest when it was built, and the harbour is expected to play a part in the planned energy island linked to Bornholm. Jack-up installation vessels, heavy-lift ships carrying turbine components and foundations, cable layers and smaller crew transfer vessels now share the port with the island's ferries. Their time in port follows project campaigns rather than timetables: a vessel may spend days loading components, or lie alongside between projects, which creates useful gauging windows on ships whose decks and cranes have carried exceptional loads for months. Owners usually want that condition known before the next contract begins.

facilities.h: Where ships are gauged at Rønne
p: The ferry berths at Rønne are worked hard. The catamarans turn round quickly between Ystad crossings and are best measured when they come off the route for maintenance, which operators normally schedule outside the summer season. The ro-pax ship on the Køge route has longer stays in Rønne, particularly overnight, and suits a defined scope of car-deck lanes, ramp structure and selected tanks. On the newer quays built for offshore wind, installation and heavy-lift vessels lie alongside during loading and between campaigns, and their open working decks and crane foundations can be reached directly from the quay or from the ship's own deck.

Bornholm has no large commercial dry dock, so full dockings of the ferries and of the wind-industry vessels are taken to yards on the mainland or abroad. Gauging at Rønne is therefore afloat work: deck, structure and tank readings on a ship lying in the harbour, ahead of a docking or between project campaigns. The island's fishing boats and small craft have slipway and workshop services in its harbours, but merchant ships needing hull work below the waterline go elsewhere. For a ship due to dock in Poland, Germany or Denmark soon after a Rønne call, readings taken on Bornholm give the yard and class a clear starting point.
list: Ystad fast-ferry berths — hull plating, wet-deck and waterjet-room structure on aluminium catamarans withdrawn for maintenance outside the summer season.
Køge ro-pax berth — car-deck, stern-ramp, ballast tank and piping gauging on the conventional ferry during overnight or planned lay-bys.
Offshore wind quays and project areas — deck, crane-pedestal and sea-fastening structure on jack-up, heavy-lift and cable-lay vessels between campaigns.
General cargo and bulk quays — hold, hatch-coaming and deck readings on coasters supplying the island.
Cruise berth — machinery-space piping and open-deck plating on cruise ships during a summer day call.

context.h: Baltic rules, Bornholm's ferry contract and wind-farm work
p: Ships at Rønne are subject to Paris MoU port state control carried out by the Danish Maritime Authority, and the passenger ferries on regular services to Ystad, Køge and Sassnitz are also inspected under the EU regime for ro-ro passenger ships and high-speed craft. The Bornholm routes are run under a public service contract with the Danish state, which sets the timetable and capacity the operator must provide; that obligation is why ferry maintenance and docking are planned so carefully, and why gauging on these ships has to fit the operator's maintenance programme exactly. High-speed craft also follow the IMO High-Speed Craft Code, and their aluminium structure is surveyed against it and the class rules.

The southern Baltic is not usually ice-bound, but ships trading from Rønne towards northern ports in winter may carry Finnish-Swedish ice class notations, and the strengthened plating on those ships has its own minimum thicknesses. For the offshore wind vessels, the main driver of inspection is the work itself rather than port rules: jack-up legs, spudcans and leg wells, crane pedestals and the deck areas where turbine components are sea-fastened carry concentrated, repeated loads. Owners frequently want crack detection at welded attachments and readings on deck plating before a vessel moves to its next campaign, and a stay at Rønne between projects is a practical time to do it.

jobs.h: Gauging jobs that come up at Rønne
jobs.p: Rønne work follows three calendars: the ferry operator's maintenance plan, the wind-farm project schedule and the cargo calls that keep the island supplied. Ferry jobs are planned months ahead and fitted into periods when a ship is withdrawn; wind-industry jobs are often requested between campaigns, sometimes at short notice once a vessel's next mobilisation date is known. For aluminium craft, the gauge is calibrated on a reference block of the right alloy before work starts, so that readings on hull and wet-deck plating can be compared with the original scantlings. Results are reported daily so the operator can decide on repairs before the ship returns to service.
list: An aluminium catamaran off the Ystad route for winter maintenance: hull plating at the waterline, wet-deck structure and waterjet-room spaces gauged against the original scantlings.
The Køge ro-pax ferry during a planned lay-by: car-deck lanes, stern-ramp structure and ballast tanks measured before its class docking.
A jack-up installation vessel between offshore wind campaigns: MPI at crane-pedestal welds and sea-fastening doublers, with deck plating gauged under the cargo areas.
A heavy-lift ship after discharging turbine components: hatch covers, tank top and deck strengthening checked for wastage and cracking.
Hold and hatch-coaming readings on a coaster delivering bulk cargo, for an owner preparing for an intermediate survey.

logistics: Bornholm Airport, just outside Rønne, has domestic flights from Copenhagen; the alternative is to travel via Copenhagen to Ystad and take the fast ferry across. Teams from India need Schengen visas, so dates for ferry maintenance periods or wind-vessel stays should be shared early. Access to the ferry terminal and the offshore wind quays is controlled, and the ship's agent or the operator arranges passes; project vessels may also require their own safety induction before the team boards.

faqs.q: Can you measure aluminium hulls on the Bornholm fast ferries?
faqs.a: Yes. Ultrasonic thickness gauges measure aluminium as readily as steel, once the instrument is set up for the alloy's sound velocity and checked on a reference block of the same material. On high-speed catamarans we typically cover hull plating near the waterline and around the jet intakes, the wet deck between the hulls and accessible internal structure, and record readings against the original scantlings from the builder's drawings.

faqs.q: When can a Bornholm ferry be taken out of service for gauging?
faqs.a: Usually outside the summer peak, when the operator can cover the timetable with the rest of its fleet. The routes are run under a public service contract, so maintenance is planned well ahead and our scope has to fit that plan. Send us the maintenance dates as soon as they are fixed, so that visas and travel can be lined up with them.

faqs.q: Do you inspect offshore wind installation vessels in Rønne?
faqs.a: We do, for the vessel owner or operator. Between campaigns, a jack-up or heavy-lift vessel alongside at Rønne can be gauged on its working deck and tanks, with magnetic particle testing at crane pedestals, sea-fastening attachments and other heavily loaded welds. Access, permits and the vessel's safety induction are arranged with the ship's management before the team arrives.

faqs.q: Is ice a concern for ships trading from Rønne?
faqs.a: Not at Rønne itself, which is normally ice-free. It matters for ships that also trade to the northern Baltic in winter under ice class. On those ships the ice belt has its own thickness requirements, and if a Rønne call falls after a winter in ice, the ice-belt plating and frames are worth adding to the scope so that damage or wear is found before the next season.
